item.title: AoS Coach on the new Sons of Behemat
item.description: Get some army building ideas from a top Warhammer Age of Sigmar player.
item.content:encoded:
The ground is shaking, the boulders are flying, and the Sons of Behemat are lumbering towards their next big scrap. Today, Anthony Magro from AoS Coach reveals the new battletome builds that could bring the biggest smash to the battlefield. 

Anthony:  The last time I wrote about the Sons of Behemat for Warhammer Community was back in 2021, when the army’s game plan was reasonably straightforward – put an enormous Mega-Gargant on an objective and ask your opponent what they planned to do about it. 

They may still prefer to settle arguments by throwing their weight around, but the new Battletome: Sons of Behemat gives them many more options than simply marching forwards and hoping something breaks.

The Sons’ defining strengths remain: gargants are enormous, hard-hitting monsters with devastating charges and enough battlefield presence to demand an immediate response. But the new battletome gives them more tools, from Ma Maegran, Boss-stompers, and Rock-hurlers to specialised units that seize objectives, bombard the enemy, screen vulnerable areas, and create openings for a gargant to strike. They still solve problems with brute force, but now they have more say in which problem gets flattened first. That opens the door to combat-focused forces, ranged armies, specialised-unit builds, and devastating all-out assaults led by Kragnos. 

Here are three mighty gatherings of gargants that could leave an unforgettable mark on the Mortal Realms. 

Sons of Behemat – 1970/2000 pts 
Battle Formation: Looting Leviathans 
Spell Lore: Lore of Behemat 
Prayer Lore: Lore of the World Titan 
Manifestation Lore: Primal Energy
Battle Tactics: Burning for Vengeance, Legend of the Parch 

General’s Regiment 
King Brodd (430) 
• General
Kraken-eater Mega-Gargant (370)
• Artefacts of Power: Krakenskin Sandals (10) 

Regiment 1
Beast-smasher Mega-Gargant (380)
• Heroic Trait:  Unreasonable Tyrant (0)
• Realm-Shaking Rampage: Earthshaking Roar (20)
Warstomper Mega-Gargant (390)
Boss-stompers (370) 

The Boss-stompers might be LITTLE by Sons of Behemat standards, but there's nothing little about what happens when three of them reach combat. This army is built around getting them there, then having the bigger gargants pile into the same fight and make an already dangerous unit considerably nastier. 

The Beast-smasher is their natural partner. Rather than simply being another Mega-Gargant sent off to smash things by itself, I want it fighting alongside the Boss-stompers. I'll often build the Beast-smasher towards STRIKE-FIRST using the army's battle traits, allowing it to swing before the Boss-stompers and use Leader of the Pack to give their melee weapons Crit (2 Hits). Earthshaking Roar can also stop the unfortunate target from using commands, which is particularly useful when you don't want All-out Defence taking some of the sting out of what's coming next. 

Looting Leviathans is my preferred battle formation for this version of the army, because once the Boss-stompers make their charge I want them getting to the thing that actually matters. Argy Bargy can add 3" to their pile-in moves for the rest of the turn, giving them a 6" pile-in, while Get to the Goods lets a charging BIG or LITTLE unit pass across enemy models in non-MONSTER units while doing so. A screen that looked perfectly sensible at the start of the Charge phase can suddenly become much less reassuring. 

LOOTING LEVIATHANS

Passive

GET TO THE GOODS

When shiny treasure or barrels of grog are sighted, these gargants wade through ranks of little 'uns without pause.

Effect: Each time a friendly BIG or LITTLE unit that charged in the same turn makes a pile-in move, that unit can pass across enemy models in non-MONSTER units.

The rest of the army helps make that engagement happen. The Warstomper can move another BIG or LITTLE unit 2D6" in the Movement phase, while the Kraken-eater and the Beast-smasher's Unreasonable Tyrant heroic trait can each add 1 to the Boss-stompers' charge roll. King Brodd can then add 1 to the Rend of their melee weapons with Power of Behemat prayer, while remaining a serious threat in his own right. 

There's even a nasty reversal if your opponent decides to charge the Boss-stompers first. Quit Hogging Da Fun! lets them bring a nearby BIG unit into the fight immediately after they attack in the enemy combat phase. On my turn, the Beast-smasher sets up the Boss-stompers. On yours, the Boss-stompers can drag one of the big lads into the punch-up with them. 

I've deliberately taken four different Mega-Gargants here to maximise their different Once Per Turn (Army) abilities, but there is another way to build the same idea. If I swapped King Brodd for Ma Maegran, I would also replace the Warstomper with a second unit of Boss-stompers. That redundancy matters because Chooser of the Mighty can sacrifice a LITTLE model to return a destroyed non-UNIQUE BIG unit, and I don't want to weaken my only Boss-Stomper unit just to bring a Mega-Gargant back. 

Either way, the plan is wonderfully straightforward – get the gang together, pick the biggest problem on the battlefield, and introduce it to an unreasonable number of clubs. 

Sons of Behemat – 1990/2000 pts 
Battle Formation: Heirs of the Old Ways 
Spell Lore: Lore of Behemat 
Prayer Lore: Brodd’s Bellows (Scourge of Aqshy) 
Manifestation Lore: Primal Energy 
Battle Tactics: Blazing Onslaught, Burning for Vengeance 

General’s Regiment 
Ma Maegran (370) 
• General 
Ancient Ghyrochs (0) 
Boss-stompers (370) 

Regiment 1 
King Brodd (430) 
Gatebreaker Mega-Gargant (400) 
• Heroic Trait:  Always First In (0) 
• Artefacts of Power: Glowy Lantern (20) 
• Realm-Shaking Rampage: Earthshaking Roar (20) 
Rock-hurlers (380) 

Sons of Behemat armies have never exactly been famous for subtle ranged warfare, but the new Rock-hurlers give you a very different way to approach the battlefield. Rather than racing everything into combat, this army wants to apply pressure from range, force the opponent to come towards you, and then let King Brodd and the Boss-stompers finish whatever survives the opening bombardment. 

The Gatebreaker is what makes that shooting package really work. Rip It Up and Chuck It lets it uproot nearby terrain and improve the Rock-hurlers' or its own shooting, giving each Rock-hurler model an extra attack with its ranged weapons. The Rock-hurlers can then adapt with Drop, Toss or Roll depending on what the turn demands with extra range when the target is keeping its distance, better accuracy when you need the damage, or Shoot in Combat when somebody inevitably decides charging the gargants will solve the problem. 

Ma Maegran fits beautifully behind that firing line. While she stays close to another Sons of Behemat Monster, The Wandering Witch makes her invisible to enemies more than 12" away, allowing her to sit behind the Gatebreaker and Rock-hurlers and concentrate on supporting the army rather than worrying about being picked off. I generally keep the Ancient Ghyrochs nearby too, using Shepherdess to increase Ma's power level and give me more magical options each turn. 

This is also where I really like bringing the Scourge of Aqshy season rules into the army. King Brodd is already a Priest, and the Glowy Lantern lets me make the Gatebreaker another one. That gives me two sources of the Rock Bottom prayer,* which grants a 6+ Ward and lets a unit ignore the effects of Battle Damaged. For an army built around several expensive gargants, keeping a wounded Mega-Gargant operating at full effectiveness while the opponent tries to weather the shooting can be enormously valuable. 

TITANIC TROPHIES

Deployment Phase

GLOWY LANTERN

Stolen from the aelves of Hysh after a botched alliance, this aetherquartz jar was at first carried around just because it was shiny. Over time, it has granted its bearer an innate power.

Effect: If this unit is a WIZARD or PRIEST, add 1 to its power level for the rest of the battle. Otherwise, pick either the WIZARD (1) or PRIEST (1) keyword. This unit has that keyword for the rest of the battle.

Heirs of the Old Ways is my preferred battle formation here. This list wants its firing lanes and support pieces operating cleanly, so being able to interfere with enemy Wizards or Priests and potentially clear away the manifestations they have summoned helps stop the army from being pinned down before it can dictate the engagement. 

Once the enemy does close the distance, that is where Brodd and the Boss-stompers take over. The shooting does not necessarily have to destroy the target outright – it just has to make the fight that follows unfair in your favour. 

You could double down and replace the Boss-stompers with another unit of Rock-hurlers, or trade them for three individual Mancrushers to gain more scoring pieces and cleaner sacrifices for Chooser of the Mighty. If you do take three Mancrushers, it is also worth considering the Hammer Throw Realm-shaking Rampage, which lets you throw a Mancrusher 3D6" and potentially launch it straight into combat. I prefer the mixed version, though. Your opponent can stay back and get rocks thrown at them, or come closer and discover that the ammunition was never the biggest threat. 

Sons of Behemat – 1960/2000 pts 
Battle Formation: Looting Leviathans 
Spell Lore: Lore of Behemat 
Prayer Lore: Lord of the World Titan 
Manifestation Lore: Aetherwrought Machineries 
Battle Tactics: Burning for Vengeance, Legend of the Parch 

General’s Regiment 
Kragnos (580) 
• General 
Beast-smasher Mega-Gargant (380) 
• Heroic Trait:  Brute of Brutes (0) 
• Artefacts of Power: Glowy Lantern (20) 
• Realm-Shaking Rampage: Earthshaking Roar (20) 

Regiment 1 
King Brodd (430) 
Scourge of Aqshy Mancrusher (150) 
• Cracked Heels: That Boy’s Not Right (10) 

Regiment 2 
Ma Maegran (370) 
Ancient Ghyrochs (0) 

Sometimes the best way to control the battlefield is to make sure your opponent never gets comfortable on it. This list is built around Kragnos doing exactly that, using his 3D6” charge support to turn the opening turns into an immediate threat while the rest of the army piles in behind him. 

King Brodd is a big part of making that happen. Through World Titan’s Stride, he can add 3" to Kragnos’ Move and let him pass across enemy models and terrain as though he had FLY. Kragnos already threatens an enormous distance thanks to those 3D6” charges, so giving him even more freedom to move around screens or awkward terrain helps make sure he reaches the fight you actually care about rather than the one your opponent wants to offer you. 

Once he gets there, the Beast-smasher and Ma Maegran start layering on the support. Leader of the Pack can give Kragnos Crit (2 Hits), while Creepy Cantrips can add 1 to hit rolls for his combat attacks. Brodd can then contribute Power of Behemat for extra Rend. I don’t need every one of those effects every turn, but having access to them means Kragnos can go from being a fast hammer to an absolutely brutal one when the right target presents itself.

MA MAEGRAN

CHOOSER OF THE MIGHTY

Your Hero Phase

CREEPY CANTRIPS

Maegran has memorised many weird, witchy cantrips and mutter-curses. If performed with enough gusto and allied to her sinister reputation, the resulting sense of menace can goad nearby gargants into terrified action.

Declare: Pick a visible friendly SONS OF BEHEMAT MONSTER unit wholly within 18" of this unit to be the target, then make a casting roll of 2D6.

Effect: Until the start of your next turn, add 1 to rampage rolls for the target and add 1 to hit rolls for the target's combat attacks.

The Beast-smasher carries the Glowy Lantern and Earthshaking Roar, giving me another Priest and a way to switch off commands on whatever I’m trying to overwhelm. Brute of Brutes helps keep its own attacks reliable, which matters because I don’t want it to be standing around as a passive support piece – it should be arriving in the same combat and helping Kragnos finish the job. 

Ma Maegran fills a different role here to the previous list. I’m less interested in hiding her behind a shooting castle and more interested in having her follow the main assault as a mobile magical support piece. The Ancient Ghyrochs help increase her power level, giving her the casting bandwidth to keep feeding useful buffs into the front line. 

The Scourge of Aqshy Mancrusher is the cheap utility piece that makes the list tick. It can contribute to mission play, dabble in prayers through That Boy’s Not Right, and since it has the LITTLE keyword it becomes an ideal sacrifice for Chooser of the Mighty if the Beast-smasher goes down. That means I can afford to throw the Beast-smasher into dangerous combats knowing Ma may be able to bring it back later. 

This isn’t the subtle Sons list. It’s the one that wants to seize the initiative, hit first, and make the opponent start solving problems immediately. 

If Kragnos is known as the End of Empires, this army is really just trying to make sure he gets started early. 

More Than A One-Hit Wonder 

These three lists only scratch the surface of what the new Sons of Behemat battletome can do. 

You can double down on Rock-hurlers and turn the army into a much heavier ranged threat, build around multiple Boss-stomper units for redundancy, lean harder into Mancrushers for mission play, or explore very different combinations of Mega-Gargants depending on which support abilities you value most. Ma Maegran alone opens up a whole range of list-building decisions around magic, LITTLE units and bringing destroyed Mega-Gargants back into the fight. 

That is probably what I like most about this battletome. There is no longer one obvious question of which Mega-Gargants hit hardest. Instead, I find myself asking which gargants I want working together, what role each one is filling, and how those pieces help the army control the battlefield. 

The Sons of Behemat are still enormous, still destructive, and still perfectly capable of solving problems by hitting them with something the size of a building. They just have a few more ways to decide which building to use. 

Thanks, Anthony! Grab the new Sons of Behemat battletome, along with Ma Maegran, and the Boss-stompers/Rock-hurlers kit, when it goes on sale tomorrow.

* Which can be found in the Scourge of Aqshy downloads.

item.title: Chronicles of Ruin – King of the Bigs
item.description: Enjoy free Warhammer Age of Sigmar fiction.
item.content:encoded:
The new Sons of Behemat miniatures and battletome are available for pre-order tomorrow! Get ready for the latest stomp with a free piece of Warhammer Age of Sigmar fiction.

King Brodd does not often dream. When he does, he dreams of the lightning.

Which is not really a surprise. He has seen plenty of lightning, raging on the horizon or being hurled by some squawking little ’un. But only one instance – one irreversible moment – is the lightning. You don’t readily forget a display of such absolute power that it burns out your eye and murders a god.

Especially when that god is your father.

But Brodd, when he bothers to acknowledge his dreams at all, reminds himself to keep quiet. There are certain things a king doesn’t talk about. There are also certain things that a proper gargant doesn’t talk about.

So, when he tells the tales to audiences of rapt, gawping gargants, Brodd doesn’t mention the lightning that crackles through his sparse dreams, though he proclaims what he intends to do to the storm-godling of Azyr viscerally and often. He describes in punishing detail how he’ll twist the Sigmar the Hammer King’s limbs off and squash him between huge, wart-encrusted toes, but he never mentions the scar in his mind’s eye. He recounts seeing Behemat, the World Titan, topple into death as Sigmar’s treacherous bolts struck him, but he says nothing of the feeling that welled in his own chest as he did so. 

Any gargant who tries to delve deeper with questions gets a scowl and a cuff round the head, at best. Brodd tells them the stories, but it is not his job to bare his soul to them. His task is vengeance – and vengeance alone.

Yet now there’s another breed of lightning, and this one does not haunt his sleep. It’s real. It crackles an evil green as it comes closer, dripping from the rusty iron fangs of the vermin-machine forcing him into the slop of the Scabrous Sprawl. Cold mud crawls up Brodd’s leg as he pushes back against that mechanised pressure. 

‘Come on,’ the lightning seems to say, ‘sleep where Behemat slept. Die where your father died.’ 

In answer, Brodd roars. Spittle flies from gaps in his teeth onto the Parasite Engine he’s wrestling with – a huge, skittering, multi-limbed mechanical monster. Ratmen swarm over the machine’s hide of scrap, adding their shrill voices to the cacophony. Brodd grits his teeth and strains at the metal limbs, bunching every muscle. His eye feels like it’s going to pop. He tries to summon up the divine strength of his forefather, but he finds it won’t come. He grunts, demanding it, and still it won’t come.

The sounds of other gargants battling against the tide of gnashing, slashing rats has grown distant. He wonders what he looks like to them. Strong? Like a king, with his veins bulging and nostrils flaring? It doesn’t matter. The Engine’s mouth is getting closer, jaws grinding open and spitting electrical hate. He might die.

And it’ll be the lightning that kills him.

‘Did ye dream last eve, Brodd of the Behemati?’

It’s Maegran who says it. The Chooser of the Mighty waits until dark has fallen and the campfire, made of three trees stacked atop one another, has burned to cold embers. Her wind-crackle voice stirs Brodd just as he was beginning to nod off. The other gargants of the war party are already asleep, their snores rumbling like the echo of some cosmic birth.

‘What?’

‘Did ye dream?’ Maegran stands at the edge of the camp, leaning on her spear and smoking a pipe carved from some ancient, mouldy bone. For all her apparent age and creaking limbs, the wyrdy-witch of the bogs has yet to actually sit down in all the time Brodd has known her. Right now, that is only about two days, but it still strikes him as off. One of her moss-furred brutes snuffles around at her feet. Maegran grasps the torc clasped around its neck and gives it a yank that is possibly meant to be affectionate.

‘No,’ Brodd lies. Unconsciously, his hand finds his great obelisk-club, patting it.

‘Liar.’ Maegran chortles and blows a smoke-ring that shimmers off into the night. When she looks back at him, there’s a snaggle-tooth sneer about her. 

‘All the kings what was dreamed. When we ruled these lands and the little ’uns knelt to us, our kings dreamed.’

‘Good fer them.’

‘That ain’t kingly, Brodd.’ She’s still smirking. It makes Brodd scowl. 

‘What’d you know about that?’

‘Told you. I spoke to ’em. The old Behemati kings. Back before there was storm gods and spiky gods; when there was real gargants to be king of.’

‘What’re we, then?’

‘You’re the boss. You tell me.’

This cyclical, riddling sort of talk that Maegran so enjoys makes Brodd’s head hurt. There’s a gabbling hiss by his left ear. One of the red-fleshed imps that always cling to him apparently has an opinion. Brodd pushes the Creeper down with a finger; it flees just in time to avoid being squashed.

Brodd’s knees protest as he stands. He steps through the mass of sleeping gargants, reminding himself with some effort not to simply stomp on his own subjects. A few sleep close to where Maegran lurks: her followers, who think her magics can make them mighty if she chooses. To Brodd, it seems stupid at best, vaguely blasphemous at worst. In the future, it might be a problem. But for now – ‘now’ being the long and vengeful present that will persist until Sigmar is bloody paste, which is all that really matters to Brodd – she is an ally. 

‘You didn’t talk to no kings of old, witch,’ Brodd says as he stomps to the edge of the clearing and stares over the marshy, misty flats below. ‘All just tales on your part.’ 

Far out in the night’s gloom, amongst the mists of the Scabrous Sprawl, light sparks a faint green. If what Maegran told him in her cave was true, then there are ratmen in the deep swamps. They seek to scavenge weapons that Brodd smashed up when they disturbed the World Titan’s slumber. Now they profane his very grave. But the Sprawl is gargant turf, hence the warband sleeping at Brodd’s back, ready to smash and bash when the light rises.

‘No?’ Maegran crows a cackle that sees several slumbering gargants grunt and turn over, landslides in miniature. ‘No wonder ye be a king! You know me better than I know myself. Even the World Titan might have rumbled approval at that.’

‘You didn’t know him, neither. I won’t hear that rot.’

‘Best hope that. Perhaps ye wouldn’t like to know what he’d have thought of all this. If he thought of you at all.’

‘What’s that, witch?’

‘Well, what’s the legend of Brodd, really? Smashing little after little in one long rage? And how often do ye think of all these oafs at yer side, battling and hanging on to your every word? What are your people in this grand stomp o’ vengeance?

It’s not the answer he expects. For a long few moments, Brodd – scowling, stomping, bellowing Brodd – doesn’t know what to say. He’s the Prophet, isn’t he? Empowered, haunted, by the scraps of their dead father’s spirit? He glances around at the sleeping mob: Odro with his perpetually drooling nose; the triplets Fog, Marog, and Babog, all slumped in a snoring heap and with the messy refuse of the humans they gobbled up smeared around their mouths; Begra, who grunts in approval at every word he says and stands beside him with arms folded like some enforcer, with that corposant scar on her gut she wears so proudly. Then he turns to Maegran, one good eye narrowed amongst his drake-skull helmet, distant lightning illuminating his face.

‘You’re a tester, Chooser of the Mighty.’

‘Is that not what I’m for, King of the Bigs? To keep all you lunks honest and worthy of yer blood?’ Maegran maintains that wry smile, but there is something off-putting in her gaze now. The many carven faces hung across her frame glare and speak not.

‘You’ve come back here, to where Behemat was shot down by those even stronger than he, to smash the rats with all that godly strength what clings to you, Brodd. And aye, that be right and proper. But bigness ain’t always just size. Sometimes, bigness be in spirit. There’ll be a moment where ye’ll have to reckon with that.’

He doesn’t like the sound of that.

‘Don’t like the sound of that.’

‘But ye’ll know it,’ Maegran says, and there’s a twinkle in her evil eye now. ‘And ye’d best be ready for it. Else ye’ll find yerself a king of naught but mud and weeds.’

For a while, Brodd forgets the conversation. It seems like meandering night-talk from the wyrdy-witch, which he’s already come to learn is par for the course. Besides, the start of next morning’s battle goes well. The mists of the Scabrous Sprawl pull in thick, as if intending to shield the gargants from view as they approach the sparks of green. Then they charge out of the murk with voices raised in hullabaloo, kicking through mobs of screaming ratmen and hurling rocks to send cannons exploding into brass scraps and splinters. 

And then, at the heart of the bog, some screeching rodent techno-warlock manages to spark enough lightning and pull enough levers to bring the Parasite Engine back to life. It rises from the mire, venting waves of poison gas. A spear of green lightning shoots out from some horn-like projector and burns through Begra’s throat. She topples backwards, a tidal wave of brackish water sploshing where she falls, and that’s it, dead, eyes dull with incomprehension as they stare skywards. Brodd is still thinking that that’s no way for a gargant to go as the Engine brings its terrible weight down towards him. He catches its clawing forelimbs just in time.

And then the lightning’s coming to kill him.

Just before the machine’s power can overwhelm him entirely, something sees it lurch with a great metallic screech. Slick, bloated vines have writhed their way out of the bog-water to wrap around one of its limbs, pulling hard enough that it loses balance. It grants reprieve, enough for Brodd to stagger back and get his footing. He hears Maegran muttering mystic chants over his shoulder, feels energy crackling off her levelled spear and off the snorting beasts at her side as she weaves her spell.

She’s saved him. It still might not matter. Those gargants who have followed him here are quivering, starting to break. Their king was almost overwhelmed. That, it seems, means something to them. The Parasite Engine regains its footing with a mechanical hiss, its armour panels flaking. Brodd can just about imagine the manic rat at its control, grinning in what it thinks is victory.

‘OI!’

Brodd roars the word like some artillery barrage. The battlefield falls still as that tectonic explosion of sound issues forth. Even the Parasite Engine seems to draw back, startled and wary. Brodd steps forward, beating his fist upon his scarred chest and snorting. Around him, the watching gargants begin to chant low and stomp their humungous feet. Normally, he finds it faintly annoying. Now, Brodd goes so far as to give a leering grin.

‘You come ’ere, rat, to gargant turf, and you think you can take what you want? Nah. Into the bogs with you lot. Down to rot and be forgotten, in the shadow of our father’s bones. As all pipsqueaks should.’

Every word is slow, and low, and clear, and mocking. It is, after a fashion, kingly. The Parasite Engine appears to take umbrage. Power crackles along its vanes and prongs once more as its mechanical rodent skull stares into Brodd’s unflinching gaze. 

Except King Brodd is already moving, faster than anything as immense as he should move. Strength rises in him again, the might of Behemat, flowing as his followers chant his name and stomp that rhythmic beat of power. Maegran’s spell-beckoned tendrils yank down on the Engine once more, pulling it further into the marsh. Its focus is broken just long enough for Brodd to take his club in a two-handed grip and swing it like a meteor.

The obelisk-club crashes into the Parasite Engine’s iron flesh and keeps going. It buckles metals and whirring motors to set off a chain of furious detonations within, gouts of warpflame incinerating wailing Skaven crew. Brodd rips its weapon out in a burst of machine guts. He lets it slam down, throwing up a torrent of filth-water. He has enough time to spit into the open jaws of the Engine before it is torn apart from within by explosions.

It takes him a moment to realise that the roar he hears isn’t only the machine bursting into flames. His gargants are chanting his name. They’ve done so many times before, but this instance feels different to Brodd. Or maybe he’s just actually listening to it for the first time. It’s the sort of thing he could get used to, if he let himself.

‘Now, there be a sight,’ Maegran says as she wades to Brodd’s side, watching with a murmur as the wreck of the Parasite Engine begins to sink into the marsh. ‘Maybe Behemat’d have looked at a thing like that.’

‘Hmm,’ Brodd grunts. ‘Kingly, were it?’

‘Oh, aye. It’s a start.’ Something in the way she says it makes Brodd chuckle, a sound strange even to him. He shakes off the last prickles of the blast and lifts his good eye. The Skaven salvagers are panicking, splashing to and fro through the waters of the Sprawl in an attempt to escape, and eager gargants are already barrelling off after them with long, ungainly strides. But some of the ratman chieftains are trying to pull them back into a semblance of order, lashing them with their tails and jabbing towards the titans with cruel spears.

‘Well, yer bigness,’ Maegran says, ‘looks like the job ain’t done yet.’

‘Good,’ Brodd says, gripping his mace in both hands once more. ‘This place belongs to the Behemati. And I’m just gettin’ warmed up.’
